overview: Storms are moving in from the Pacific in a series, favoring the northwest and the Sierra early in the week. The Southern Rockies get snow Wednesday, and the Weather Prediction Center expects heavy snow and rain for southern California Tuesday.

regions.title: Cascades
regions.text: A weak ridge brings a brief dry spell Saturday, then an active pattern returns with a series of systems. Snow is light at the passes early Sunday, and forecasters say the storm track could shift toward the coast or the interior. Mt. Baker's top day is Monday, and the NWS calls for more snow there Monday through Wednesday night, 8 to 16 inches.

regions.title: Eastern Sierra
regions.text: Strong winds hit the Sierra Sunday ahead of a storm, with gusts over ridges reaching 80 mph. Rain falls in the valleys and snow in the mountains from Sunday into early Wednesday, with snow levels dropping as low as 6,500 feet. Mammoth's biggest day is Monday, and the NWS calls for more snow Sunday night through Tuesday, 5 to 12 inches.

regions.title: Tahoe
regions.text: A wet, unsettled pattern arrives Sunday and runs into midweek, with breezy south winds and gusts of 40 to 55 mph over the Sierra crest. Snow falls above about 7,500 feet. Sugar Bowl's biggest day is Sunday, and the NWS calls for more snow at Kirkwood Sunday through Tuesday, 5 to 15 inches.

regions.title: Southern Rockies
regions.text: Strong northwest winds bring snow to the central mountains through Saturday night, and a cold front brings gusts of 55 to 65 mph across the plains. Quieter weather follows early next week. Wolf Creek's biggest day is Wednesday, with snow showers forecast for Wednesday and Wednesday night.

regions.title: Coast Mountains
regions.text: Rain dominates the coast most days, with snow limited to higher terrain. Cypress Mountain's biggest day is Monday, with rain expected. Whistler has a chance of showers through midweek.

ahead.text: The Climate Prediction Center's 6-10 day outlook favors above-normal precipitation for much of the Lower 48 from around Thursday Dec 3 through Monday Dec 7. Its forecast is weaker for the Pacific Northwest, where it leans near normal.

sources.name: NOAA buoys 51001 / 51101 (method: Powder Buoy, Mike Ruzek)

buoy.text: Buoys 51001 and 51101 near Hawaii popped Nov 25, the swell signal Powder Buoy watches for a Wasatch storm about two weeks later — here Dec 6–12. In past winters a pop raised the chance of a Wasatch storm in that window by roughly 6 to 12 points. Experimental: promising, not proven.
